title: Jumping on the Clouds
directAnswer: Greedily jump 2 whenever the cloud two ahead is safe (c[i+2] == 0), otherwise jump 1. Each jump counts as one move; the safe-2-first greedy is provably optimal because you can never lose by skipping a cloud you don't have to land on. O(n) time, O(1) space.

rules: Thunderclouds (`c[i] == 1`) can **never** be landed on — jumps must skip over them.
**Prefer the 2-jump** whenever `c[i+2] == 0`; it covers more ground in the same one move.
A `2`-jump is allowed even if `c[i+1] == 1` — you fly *over* the thundercloud, you don't land on it.
Stop when you reach the **last** index `n − 1`; the loop condition is `i < n − 1`, not `i < n`.
The first and last clouds are **always** safe (`0`) per the constraints — no need to guard the start.
Every move costs exactly **1**, whether you step 1 or 2 — minimise the *number* of moves, not distance.
whenToUse: Reach the end of a line in the fewest steps with a small fixed step set
A local 'take the biggest legal step' choice is provably globally optimal
Obstacles forbid certain landing positions but the step set is tiny (1 or 2)
You want O(1) space and a single forward pass
antiSignals: Step sizes vary per cell or are large/arbitrary → general DP / BFS (Jump Game II)
You must count distinct paths, not the minimum → DP, not greedy
Costs differ per cell → shortest-path / weighted DP
Greedy choice can be locally good but globally bad → prove it or use DP
remember.takeaway: When the step set is {1, 2} and bigger steps are never harmful, greedily take the largest legal jump — it matches the DP optimum without a table. The same 'jump 2 when you safely can' instinct generalises to Jump Game and climbing-stairs-with-obstacles problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise the greedy choice (always jump 2 over a safe landing) is optimal, and whether you handle the 'fly over a thundercloud' nuance — a 2-jump only cares about the landing cloud, not the one skipped.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Checking c[i+1] before allowing a 2-jump (you don't land there, so it's irrelevant), or looping while i < n and overshooting past the last cloud.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the greedy rule, justify why jumping 2 can never be worse, and mention the equivalent O(n) DP (minJumps[i] = 1 + min(reachable)) as the safety net when greedy correctness is unclear.

problemStatement:
There is a game where you start at cloud `0` and want to reach the last cloud. The clouds are given as an array `c` where `c[i] = 0` is a *cumulus* cloud (safe to land on) and `c[i] = 1` is a *thundercloud* (cannot be landed on).

From any cloud `i` you may jump to cloud `i + 1` or cloud `i + 2`, as long as the cloud you land on is safe. Each jump counts as one move. Determine the **minimum number of jumps** required to reach the last cloud. It is guaranteed that a path exists and the first and last clouds are safe.
constraints: c[0] = 0 and c[n − 1] = 0 (start and end are always safe)
There are never two adjacent thunderclouds, so a path always exists
understanding: Walk from cloud 0 to cloud n−1 in as few jumps as possible. At each cloud you may advance by 1 or 2, but you may only land on a 0. A 2-jump passes over the intermediate cloud and only requires the destination to be safe. Minimise the count of jumps.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I jump 2 even if the cloud in between is a thundercloud?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A 2-jump only requires the landing cloud (i+2) to be safe; you fly over i+1 regardless of its value.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the first and last clouds guaranteed safe?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. c[0] = 0 and c[n−1] = 0, and no two thunderclouds are adjacent, so a valid path always exists.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it ever better to take a 1-jump when a 2-jump is available?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Since both cost one move, covering more ground with a safe 2-jump never increases the total — greedy is optimal here.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I count jumps or clouds visited?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Jumps (moves). Visiting k+1 clouds along a path means k jumps.

0→2 (c[2]=0 safe), 2→3 (c[4]=1 so can't 2-jump), 3→5 (over thundercloud at 4). Jumps = 3.

approaches.name: Greedy — Jump 2 When Safe (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this; it is the intended O(n)/O(1) answer. Justify why greedy is correct, don't just assert it.
hints: Both a 1-jump and a 2-jump cost the same single move. If a longer jump is legal, can taking it ever hurt you?
From cloud i, prefer to land on i+2 whenever c[i+2] is safe (0); the cloud at i+1 doesn't matter because you fly over it.
Walk an index forward: if i+2 is in range and safe, advance by 2, else advance by 1; increment a jump counter each time. Stop at the last index.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The index only moves forward and advances by at least 1 each iteration, so the loop runs at most n times → O(n). A handful of scalar variables → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Model the position as a single index `i` starting at 0 and a `jumps` counter at 0. Each iteration, look two ahead: if `i + 2` is within bounds and `c[i + 2] == 0`, jump there; otherwise step to `i + 1`. Count the jump and repeat until `i` reaches the last cloud.

**Why greedy is correct here.** This is the crux the interviewer wants you to defend. Every jump — whether of size 1 or 2 — costs exactly one move. So to minimise the number of moves you want each move to cover as much ground as legally possible. A 2-jump lands strictly further than a 1-jump and never blocks a future move: from any safe cloud you can always still take a 1-jump, so reaching cloud `i + 2` keeps every option open that cloud `i + 1` would have, and then some. Therefore preferring the 2-jump can never increase the total count — the greedy choice is *exchange-argument* optimal.

**Why the intermediate cloud is irrelevant.** A 2-jump from `i` lands on `i + 2`; you never set foot on `i + 1`. So `c[i + 1]` — thundercloud or not — places no constraint on the 2-jump. Beginners add a spurious `c[i+1] == 0` check and miss that flying over a thundercloud is exactly what the rules permit.

**Why the loop stops at `n − 1`.** The goal is the last index, not past it. The condition `while i < n − 1` halts the instant we land on the final cloud. Using `i < n` would let the index walk off the end and over-count. Because the constraints forbid two adjacent thunderclouds and guarantee `c[0] = c[n−1] = 0`, the greedy walk can always make legal progress and will always terminate exactly on the last cloud.
approaches.insight: When all moves cost the same and a bigger move never removes a future option, 'take the biggest legal step' is provably optimal — no DP table needed. The exchange argument (a longer jump dominates a shorter one) is the one-sentence proof to say out loud.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming — Minimum Jumps Table
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the rigorous fallback when you can't immediately prove greedy is optimal, or as a lead-in to the generalised Jump Game II.
hints: Define dp[i] = minimum jumps to reach cloud i. What are the only clouds you could have jumped FROM to land on i?
You arrive at i from i-1 or i-2 (whichever are safe and in range): dp[i] = 1 + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]).
Set dp[0] = 0, skip thunderclouds (leave them unreachable / infinity), and return dp[n-1].
approaches.complexityReasoning: Filling the table is a single left-to-right pass with O(1) work per cloud → O(n) time. The dp array of size n → O(n) space (reducible to O(1) by keeping only the last two values).
approaches.explanation:
Dynamic programming makes the optimality airtight without an exchange argument. Let `dp[i]` be the minimum number of jumps needed to reach cloud `i`, with `dp[0] = 0`.

**The recurrence.** You can only land on cloud `i` (a safe cloud) from cloud `i − 1` or cloud `i − 2`. So `dp[i] = 1 + min(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2])`, taking only those predecessors that are in range and reachable. Thunderclouds are never destinations, so we leave their `dp` as infinity (unreachable) — they simply don't contribute as predecessors when their own value is computed, but a 2-jump *over* them still works because `dp[i]` may draw from `dp[i − 2]` while `dp[i − 1]` is infinity.

**Why it agrees with greedy.** Because every edge has weight 1, the shortest path the DP finds equals the greedy move count. The DP is more general — it would still be correct if costs varied or if greedy were *not* obviously optimal — which is exactly why it's the safe choice to mention when you're unsure. For this specific problem greedy wins on space (`O(1)` vs `O(n)`), so state DP as the conceptual backbone and greedy as the optimised realisation.

**Space reduction.** Since `dp[i]` depends only on the previous two entries, you can collapse the array to two rolling variables and recover `O(1)` space — at which point it's essentially the greedy loop wearing a DP hat.
approaches.insight: Minimum-jumps problems are shortest-path problems on a tiny graph: dp[i] = 1 + min over legal predecessors. Recognising 'fewest moves' as 'shortest path with unit edges' is the transferable idea — it scales to Jump Game II and grid BFS.

commonMistakes: Requiring c[i+1] to be safe before a 2-jump — you fly over it, so only c[i+2] matters.
Looping while i < n instead of i < n - 1, causing an overshoot and an extra jump.
Confusing 'minimum jumps' with 'maximum distance' — every jump costs one move regardless of length.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Blocking a 2-jump on the skipped cloud
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A 2-jump lands on i+2 and never touches i+1, so c[i+1] is irrelevant. Checking it prevents valid jumps over thunderclouds.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if i + 2 < n and c[i + 1] == 0 and c[i + 2] == 0:
    i += 2
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if i + 2 < n and c[i + 2] == 0:
    i += 2

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong loop bound overshoots the end
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping while i < n lets the index step past the last cloud and counts a phantom extra jump. Stop at n - 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow with INF sentinel (DP)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Using Integer.MAX_VALUE as INF and then adding 1 wraps to a large negative number, corrupting the min.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
// ... dp[i] = INF + 1;  // overflow!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE / 2;
// ... dp[i] = best + 1;  // safe

patternNote: Greedy maximal step on a line with a {1,2} step set. When every move costs the same and a longer legal jump never closes off a future option, greedily take the biggest legal jump — it equals the unit-edge shortest path (DP). Generalises to Jump Game and stair-climbing problems.
